cards.q: In what sense is a database isolation level a memory model?
cards.a: Both are specifications of which interleavings a participant may observe. Read committed permits non-repeatable reads, the database equivalent of a compiler not being required to re-read a variable; Postgres SERIALIZABLE uses optimistic concurrency and can abort you with a serialization failure requiring the same retry loop as CAS.

cards.q: How is an idempotency key a compare-and-swap?
cards.a: A retry racing an original is the same interleaving problem; checking and inserting the key atomically is compare-and-swap over the network. Once you have seen the pattern at the instruction level the distributed version needs no separate learning.

cards.q: When is a spin lock right and when is it catastrophic?
cards.a: Right when hold time is shorter than a context switch — a few hundred nanoseconds — and there are more cores than contenders, which is true inside a kernel and almost never in application code. Catastrophic on a single core: the spinner cannot progress until the holder runs, and the holder cannot run until the spinner is preempted.

cards.q: Why is test and test-and-set better than plain test-and-set?
cards.a: Spinning on a write means each attempt acquires the cache line exclusively, saturating the interconnect and slowing the actual holder. Spinning on a plain read can be satisfied from a shared line, and only the final attempt writes.

cards.q: What is the futex's key property?
cards.a: The uncontended path never enters the kernel. Acquire is a compare-and-swap in user space — a few nanoseconds; only on failure does it call futex(FUTEX_WAIT, ...) to sleep on a kernel wait queue keyed by that address. Release wakes only if it can see a waiter.

cards.q: Why is a high futex count in strace -c meaningful?
cards.a: Because uncontended locks make no system calls at all, so futex calls are direct evidence of genuine contention.

cards.q: What is a semaphore and how does it relate to a mutex?
cards.a: Dijkstra, 1965: a counter with atomic decrement-and-wait-if-negative and increment-and-wake. Initialised to N it permits N holders, which makes it the natural expression of a resource pool. A mutex is the case N=1.

cards.q: Why must a condition variable always be waited on in a while loop?
cards.a: Because of spurious wakeups, and because another thread may have consumed the condition before you were scheduled.

cards.q: Name Coffman's four conditions for deadlock and say which one you break.
cards.a: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. In practice you break circular wait, with lock ordering: define a total order over all locks and always acquire in it — which is why multi-row database code should sort identifiers first.

cards.q: Distinguish deadlock, livelock, starvation and the thundering herd.
cards.a: Deadlock: nothing runs. Livelock: threads run and respond to each other but nothing completes. Starvation: a thread never gets the resource because others keep taking it. Thundering herd: releasing wakes every waiter, all of whom race and all but one sleep again — hence waking one.

cards.q: Why is Redis single-threaded, and what is the price?
cards.a: Every command is atomic by construction — no locks, races, deadlock or coherence traffic — which is why INCR is a correct distributed counter and a Lua script is atomic. The price is that one slow command blocks everything (KEYS * on a large database is an outage, hence SCAN) and that commands use one core. Redis 6 threaded the socket I/O while keeping execution single-threaded.

cards.q: How do you diagnose a lock wait in Postgres?
cards.a: pg_stat_activity: wait_event_type = 'Lock' means waiting on another transaction, 'LWLock' means internal shared memory. pg_blocking_pids() names the blocker. Postgres detects deadlocks after deadlock_timeout (1 s) and aborts one transaction with an error you can catch and retry — unusually generous; most systems just hang.

cards.q: Why is a distributed lock not a lock?
cards.a: Nothing guarantees the holder has not vanished. A GC pause, CPU throttling or a partition can exceed the lease, after which two processes believe they hold it. The fix is a fencing token — a monotonically increasing number passed with every write and rejected by the storage layer if lower than the highest seen. Without fencing it reduces contention rather than guaranteeing correctness.

cards.q: Why does async-mutex work without atomics, and where does it fail?
cards.a: It is a promise chain, and JavaScript's run-to-completion means the acquire check and set cannot be interleaved. It is correct within one Node process and gives you exactly nothing across cluster workers or replicas.

cards.q: What actually happens when a process blocks on read?
cards.a: The syscall enters the kernel; the socket buffer is empty; the task's state becomes S; it is added to that socket's wait queue; the scheduler picks something else. Later a packet arrives, the kernel walks the wait queue and marks the task runnable, and it eventually copies the bytes and returns.

cards.q: Correct the claim that blocking wastes CPU.
cards.a: A blocked process consumes exactly zero processor time. The cost is not cycles — it is that this thread can do nothing else, so many clients need many threads, and threads are the expensive thing.

cards.q: Name the three pre-event-loop server architectures and what each traded.
cards.a: Process per connection (inetd, Apache prefork): robust, a crash contained, and expensive. Thread per connection (Apache worker, classic servlet containers): cheaper, still a stack and a scheduler entry each. Bounded thread pool: bounds resource use and introduces head-of-line blocking.

cards.q: Run the C10K arithmetic for thread-per-connection.
cards.a: ~100 KB per thread all-in is 1 GB of memory before any application data; ten thousand tasks in the scheduler; and at ten events per second per connection, 100,000 wake-ups per second at a few microseconds each — a large fraction of a core spent purely switching. Worst of all, the caches never hold anything useful.

cards.q: State the event loop's advantage and its exact boundary.
cards.a: One thread learns about many ready connections in one call and handles each with a function call: nanoseconds and warm caches, and a few hundred bytes per connection instead of ~100 KB. It says nothing about computation — if each event needs 10 ms of processing, one thread handles a hundred per second.

cards.q: Why was nginx written, and what did it beat Apache at?
cards.a: Igor Sysoev, released October 2004, specifically against C10K: an event-driven architecture with one worker process per core. Under many idle or slow connections — which is what the real internet is — it used a fraction of the memory and stayed responsive where Apache thrashed.

cards.q: What was Ryan Dahl's stated argument for Node.js in 2009?
cards.a: That Apache's concurrency model was wrong, and that existing languages made non-blocking code painful because they had blocking standard libraries and no natural callback idiom. JavaScript had no I/O library to deprecate and already had closures.

cards.q: What makes Node's non-blocking guarantee actually hold?
cards.a: That there is no alternative — a library cannot accidentally block the loop with a blocking read because the blocking read is not exposed. Except the Sync functions, which is why using them outside startup is the cardinal error.

cards.q: Why is a database connection pool a bounded thread pool?
cards.a: It has all the same properties: 20 connections serving 200 concurrent requests means 180 waiting, invisibly, inside your process; and one slow query holds a connection while everything behind it waits — head-of-line blocking. Instrument acquisition wait time and queue depth, use statement timeouts, and separate pools for fast and slow work.

cards.q: Why does Slowloris defeat thread-per-connection and not an event loop?
cards.a: Each slowly-held connection occupies a thread in the first design, so a few hundred exhaust the pool with almost no bandwidth. In an event loop each costs a socket and a few hundred bytes. Header and body timeouts still exist because the resource is small but not zero.

cards.q: Why is a 200 ms JSON.parse categorically different in Node than in a threaded server?
cards.a: In thread-per-connection it delays one client. In an event loop it delays every client, because there is one thread and it is not preemptible. Measuring it is what monitorEventLoopDelay is for — the single most valuable metric a Node service can export.

cards.q: Why is a loop over ten thousand non-blocking descriptors not a solution?
cards.a: It makes ten thousand system calls per pass and almost all return EAGAIN. At 50–100 ns each, one pass costs a millisecond of pure overhead and typically finds nothing.

cards.q: Name select's three structural problems.
cards.a: FD_SETSIZE is 1024, compiled into the bitmap type; you rebuild and re-pass the entire set every call because the call destroys it, and the kernel copies and scans all of it; and the return tells you how many are ready, not which, so you scan all n again.

cards.q: State the wrong scaling property in one sentence.
cards.a: The cost is proportional to the number of connections you have rather than the number of events that happened — which is exactly wrong for servers holding many mostly-idle connections.

cards.q: What did poll fix and what did it leave?
cards.a: It replaced the fixed-size bitmap with an array that is not destroyed, so there is no 1024 limit and no rebuilding. The array is still passed in full, copied, and scanned every call. An ergonomic improvement, not an architectural one.

cards.q: How does epoll achieve O(1), mechanically?
cards.a: Registering a descriptor attaches a callback to that socket's wait queue. When the network softirq appends data, that callback pushes the descriptor onto the epoll instance's ready list. So the list is maintained continuously by the events themselves, and epoll_wait does not scan — it hands back the list.

cards.q: Distinguish level-triggered from edge-triggered, and say who uses which.
cards.a: Level-triggered reports readiness as long as data remains, so a partial read is safe. Edge-triggered reports only the transition, so failing to drain to EAGAIN means the connection hangs silently — faster, and unforgiving. libuv is level-triggered; nginx is edge-triggered.

cards.q: Name the four platform mechanisms libuv hides.
cards.a: epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD/macOS, Jonathan Lemon, FreeBSD 4.1, 2000 — arguably a better design, handling timers, signals and file events through one interface), IOCP (Windows, completion-based rather than readiness-based), and Solaris event ports.

cards.q: Why can a regular file not be polled for readiness?
cards.a: Readiness answers 'will this block?', and for a file the answer is always that you can read it — the real question is how long, which readiness cannot express. epoll returns EPERM for regular files, and O_NONBLOCK is simply ignored on them.

cards.q: Given that, what are the only three possible responses, and which did Node take?
cards.a: Use threads (libuv's threadpool — Node's answer, and the reason UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE exists); use POSIX aio, widely regarded as broken; or use io_uring, a completion-based interface that works properly, which libuv adopted for some file operations from 1.45 (2023).

cards.q: What does strace on an idle Node server show, and what does that tell you?
cards.a: One line: a blocked epoll_wait. That is the entire runtime at rest, consuming zero CPU. Under load it becomes epoll_wait returning, a burst of read/write/futex, and back.

cards.q: Why can a slow DNS server stall your file reads?
cards.a: dns.lookup calls getaddrinfo, a blocking library function, so it runs on the shared libuv threadpool alongside file I/O, crypto and zlib. Four threads by default. Use dns.resolve, which speaks DNS over a socket and goes through epoll.

cards.q: What is EMFILE, why is 1024 the classic limit, and how do you diagnose it?
cards.a: The per-process descriptor table is full. 1024 is a fossil of select's FD_SETSIZE. Diagnose with ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l and lsof -p; usually it is a leak — unconsumed HTTP responses, unclosed streams, connections without keep-alive timeouts — and a leak exhausts any limit.

cards.q: What is backpressure at the socket level, and what happens if you ignore it?
cards.a: A full send buffer makes a non-blocking write return short, and the correct response is to register for EPOLLOUT. Node surfaces this as write() returning false and a later 'drain'. Ignoring it means Node buffers the unwritten data in your heap without limit — which is how streaming a large file to a slow client exhausts memory. pipeline() handles it, which is the real reason to prefer it.

cards.q: What kind of thing is the event loop, precisely?
cards.a: A scheduler in user space. Everything from Node 7 applies, with one decisive difference: it has no timer interrupt and no privileged mode, so it is cooperative and regains control only when a callback returns.

cards.q: Name libuv's phases in order.
cards.a: timers; pending callbacks (deferred system operations, chiefly certain TCP errors); idle and prepare (internal); poll (the only phase that blocks); check (setImmediate); close callbacks.

cards.q: How is the poll timeout computed, in three cases?
cards.a: Zero if setImmediate callbacks are pending, since the check phase has work. The time until the nearest timer if any — which is how setTimeout is implemented, with no timer syscall and no timer thread. Otherwise infinite, which is why an idle Node process uses zero CPU.

cards.q: Why does a Node process exit, and why does a forgotten setInterval prevent it?
cards.a: There is no 'main is finished' concept — the loop exits when nothing at all is pending: no handles, no requests, no timers. A live timer or an unclosed server is pending work.

cards.q: Where do process.nextTick and microtasks run?
cards.a: Not in any phase — after every single callback and between every phase transition, drained completely including anything added while draining. nextTick first, entirely, then microtasks, entirely.

cards.q: How can process.nextTick hang a process?
cards.a: A nextTick that schedules another loops forever without the loop advancing: no I/O served, no timers, apparently hung at 100% CPU. The same is true of a recursively resolving promise chain. setImmediate cannot do this because it lands in the next iteration's check phase.

cards.q: Where does the code after an await run relative to timers and I/O?
cards.a: Before both. The continuation is queued as a microtask, so await is a very cheap yield rather than a trip through the loop. await on a non-promise still yields and still costs a microtask turn.

cards.q: Why is setTimeout(f,0) vs setImmediate(g) nondeterministic at the top level but deterministic inside an I/O callback?
cards.a: At the top level the 1 ms clamp may or may not have elapsed by the time the loop first reaches timers, depending on startup duration. Inside an I/O callback the loop is in the poll phase and check comes immediately after, while timers are a full iteration away — so setImmediate always wins.

cards.q: Describe one iteration of the browser's event loop.
cards.a: Take one task from a task queue and run it to completion; perform a microtask checkpoint, draining that queue entirely; then, if it is time to render, run the rendering steps.

cards.q: Name the browser's rendering steps in order.
cards.a: requestAnimationFrame callbacks; recalculate style; layout; update the compositing tree; paint. Then requestIdleCallback if time remains before the next frame.

cards.q: Why is requestAnimationFrame the correct place for visual changes and setTimeout(f,16) not?
cards.a: rAF runs immediately before style and layout, so changes are applied in the same frame with no intermediate paint. A timer lands in a task queue with no relationship to the frame boundary, producing jitter and dropped frames.

cards.q: What is layout thrashing and why does batching fix it?
cards.a: Reading a geometric property (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop) forces the browser to flush pending style and layout to answer correctly. Alternating writes and reads forces a layout per iteration; all reads then all writes makes it one.

cards.q: Why does React's scheduler use MessageChannel rather than setTimeout?
cards.a: To avoid the 4 ms clamp on nested timeouts. It yields roughly every 5 ms so the browser can take input and paint — a cooperative scheduler inside a cooperative scheduler inside a preemptive one.

cards.q: What are event loop delay and event loop utilisation, and why export both?
cards.a: Delay is the time between when a callback was due and when it ran — it tells you whether the loop is being blocked and by how much. Utilisation is the fraction of time the loop spent working rather than waiting in epoll_wait — it tells you how close to saturated the process is, and is a better autoscaling signal than CPU. A p99 delay of 200 ms at 40% CPU is a complete diagnosis.

cards.q: List everything that blocks the event loop.
cards.a: Any *Sync call; JSON.parse/stringify on a large object; synchronous crypto or compression; a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS); a large synchronous loop; a deep structuredClone; template rendering of a large page; and a very large number of pending microtasks, since they drain fully before the loop advances.

cards.q: Match the fixes to the causes.
cards.a: Chunk with setImmediate to yield between chunks; move CPU-bound work to a worker thread; move heavy or slow work to a separate process or a queue; stream instead of buffering; or push it into the database if it is really a data operation. Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE does nothing for main-thread blocking.

cards.q: What is Unix's definition of a file, and why was it radical?
cards.a: A finite sequence of bytes, and nothing more — no records, no line structure, no type the system knows. Contemporary systems like OS/360 had record-oriented files whose format the system enforced. Throwing that away is what makes any program's output usable as any other's input, and it is the root of the pipe-based toolchain.

cards.q: What is an inode, and what is not in it?
cards.a: A fixed-size on-disk record holding the file's type, permissions, owner, size, timestamps, link count and data block pointers. The name is not in it — names live in directories.

cards.q: What is a directory?
cards.a: A file whose contents are a list of name-to-inode-number pairs. Nothing more.

cards.q: Why is deleting called unlink?
cards.a: It removes a directory entry and decrements the inode's link count. The data is freed only when the count reaches zero and no process still holds the file open.

cards.q: You deleted a 40 GB log and df still shows the disk full. Why, and what do you do?
cards.a: A running process still has it open, so the link count reached zero but the reference count did not. lsof | grep deleted finds the holder; restart or signal it, or truncate the file rather than deleting it next time.

cards.q: Why is write-temp-then-rename the standard safe-write idiom?
cards.a: rename() is atomic with respect to readers: they see either the whole old file or the whole new one, never a partial write. It works because an open file has no name — a reader holding the old inode is unaffected.

cards.q: Contrast hard links and symbolic links.
cards.a: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode — equally the file, sharing permissions, unable to cross filesystems or point at directories (cycles). A symlink is a tiny file whose contents are a path string, resolved at every use — so it can cross filesystems, can dangle, and adds a resolution step.

cards.q: How can a disk with free space refuse writes with ENOSPC?
cards.a: Inode exhaustion. Traditional filesystems allocate a fixed inode table at format time, so millions of tiny files can use them all. df -h shows space free; df -i shows the truth.

cards.q: Name four things that are files but are not files.
cards.a: Devices (/dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/urandom, /dev/sda); pipes and sockets; kernel state (/proc, /sys — reading executes kernel code that generates the content); and terminals. The payoff is that every tool written for files works on all of it.

cards.q: What is the VFS and what does it make possible?
cards.a: A kernel layer defining operations (look up, read, write, create) that every filesystem implements — introduced by Sun in 1985 for NFS. It is why ext4, XFS, NFS, tmpfs, overlayfs, procfs and FUSE all live in one tree, and why mount can attach any filesystem at any point.

cards.q: What is a bind mount, and why does it hide things?
cards.a: The same inodes appearing at a second location in the tree — no copy, no sync, literally the same files. A mount replaces what a path resolves to, so bind-mounting your source over /app hides the image's /app/node_modules; an anonymous volume at that deeper path shadows the first mount, which is why that trick works.

cards.q: Why does moving a file from /tmp to a volume behave differently from moving within it?
cards.a: rename across filesystems fails with EXDEV, so the library falls back to copy-then-delete, which is not atomic. Upload handling should write the temporary file into the destination filesystem.

cards.q: Why does a dev server on a big repo fail with ENOSPC when there is plenty of disk?
cards.a: inotify watch limits — fs.inotify.max_user_watches, historically 8192. It is one of the most misleading error codes in Linux, since no space is involved.

cards.q: What problem is pnpm solving, in this node's terms?
cards.a: Hundreds of thousands of small files are slow to create, slow to traverse, slow to send as build context, and inode-hungry. pnpm keeps one content-addressed store and hard-links into each project, so a file exists once on disk with many names; Yarn PnP eliminates the directory entirely.

cards.q: Describe the three tables behind a file descriptor.
cards.a: The per-process descriptor table (the small integer indexes it, and entries hold a pointer plus close-on-exec); the system-wide open file table, where each open file description holds the offset, access mode and status flags; and the inode table. Collapsing these to one is the source of every confusion about descriptors.

cards.q: Why does opening a file twice give independent offsets while fork gives a shared one?
cards.a: Two open calls create two open file descriptions. dup and fork create two descriptors pointing at one description — so a parent and child writing to inherited stdout interleave correctly rather than overwriting each other. That is the reason for the design.

cards.q: Why are stdout and stderr separate descriptors?
cards.a: So results and complaints can go to different places — which is what makes ./build > out.log 2> err.log possible and why error messages still reach your terminal when output is piped.

cards.q: Which one-line specification makes shell redirection possible?
cards.a: open always returns the lowest-numbered unused descriptor. Close descriptor 1, then open the file: it becomes descriptor 1.

cards.q: Derive ls > out.txt.
cards.a: fork; in the child, dup2 the opened file onto descriptor 1 (or close 1 then open); execve /bin/ls, which keeps descriptors. ls writes to 1 as always, knowing nothing. Redirection is descriptor-table rearrangement in the gap between fork and exec.

cards.q: What are a pipe's three blocking behaviours, and what does each give you?
cards.a: Writing to a full pipe blocks — that is backpressure built into the primitive. Reading an empty one blocks until data or until all write ends close, giving end-of-file. Writing with no readers raises SIGPIPE, which is why yes | head -5 terminates: producers die when consumers stop caring.

cards.q: Why does a shell script sometimes hang waiting on a pipe that should have ended?
cards.a: Some process still holds a write end open — often an inherited descriptor a subshell forgot to close — so the reader never sees EOF.

cards.q: Derive cmd1 | cmd2.
cards.a: Create a pipe; fork twice; in the first child dup2(fds[1], 1) and close both original ends; in the second dup2(fds[0], 0) and close both; exec both. Two unmodified programs connected using nothing but the descriptor table.

cards.q: What does the stdio option in child_process actually specify?
cards.a: The child's descriptor table. 'pipe' creates a pipe and gives you a stream; 'inherit' passes your own descriptor through so the child writes directly to your terminal or log with no relaying; 'ignore' opens /dev/null; and 'ipc' as a fourth entry is the message channel child_process.fork() uses.

cards.q: Explain the classic subprocess deadlock and its two fixes.
cards.a: The child produces 10 MB on stdout, the parent waits for exit before reading; the pipe fills at 64 KB, the child blocks writing, the parent blocks waiting. It is a bounded-queue deadlock. Fixes: consume output continuously (spawn with streams), or accept exec's maxBuffer limit and its ENOBUFS.

cards.q: Why does the 12-factor rule about logging to stdout matter mechanically?
cards.a: Docker gives PID 1 a pipe for stdout and stderr and reads from it. Writing to a file inside the container bypasses all of it, so docker logs and every shipper see nothing. It also means a stalled log consumer fills the pipe and your application blocks on console.log.

cards.q: What is close-on-exec and why does it matter for security?
cards.a: Without FD_CLOEXEC, every descriptor you hold is inherited by every subprocess — including database connections, key files, and listening sockets, so a subprocess can read from an already-authenticated socket. Modern APIs default to it, which is why deliberately passing a descriptor (cluster, systemd socket activation) requires clearing it.

cards.q: Give the two numbers that shape database design.
cards.a: A hard disk random read is a seek (4–10 ms) plus half a rotation (4.2 ms at 7200 rpm) — around 8–12 ms. Sequential transfer once positioned is 100–200 MB/s. The ratio is roughly 100 to 1.

cards.q: Name three database designs that exist because of that ratio.
cards.a: B-trees, to keep seeks logarithmic; write-ahead logs, to convert random writes into sequential ones; and the planner's preference for a sequential scan past a certain selectivity, encoded as random_page_cost 4.0 against seq_page_cost 1.0 — which is why lowering it to ~1.1 on SSD is standard and changes plans.

cards.q: Why does an SSD contain a translation layer?
cards.a: Flash is read and written in 4–16 KB pages but erased only in multi-megabyte blocks, and pages cannot be overwritten in place. So the Flash Translation Layer maps logical addresses to physical pages, writing to fresh pages and garbage-collecting stale blocks in the background.

cards.q: Name three consequences of the FTL you can observe.
cards.a: Write amplification (writing 4 KB causes far more flash traffic); latency spikes when garbage collection collides with your writes, so p99 is much worse than the average; and the need for TRIM, without which a full-then-emptied SSD stays slow.

cards.q: State the latency hierarchy from L1 to a cross-continent round trip.
cards.a: L1 ~1 ns; L2 ~4 ns; DRAM ~80 ns; NVMe ~20–80 µs; SATA SSD ~100 µs; same-datacentre network ~100–500 µs; disk seek ~5–10 ms; cross-continent ~100 ms.

cards.q: Why is the modern I/O scheduler for an NVMe device none?
cards.a: The elevator algorithm existed to avoid pathological head movement on spinning disks. NVMe devices have thousands of deep queues and reorder better internally than the kernel can.

cards.q: Where are your bytes after write() returns, and what survives what?
cards.a: In the kernel page cache: survives a process crash including SIGKILL, lost on power failure or panic. Before that they may still be in your language's buffer, lost on a process crash. After writeback they are in the device's volatile write cache, still lost on power failure. Only the medium survives everything.

cards.q: What does fsync guarantee, and what does fdatasync skip?
cards.a: It writes back all dirty pages of that file and issues a cache-flush to the device, returning only when the device says the data is durable. fdatasync may skip metadata that does not affect reading the data back, and is what databases usually use.

cards.q: Why is fsync the most important number in database performance?
cards.a: An in-memory row insert is a microsecond; a committed durable insert is bounded below by one fsync — milliseconds on a disk, tens to hundreds of microseconds on a consumer SSD, near zero on enterprise hardware with power-loss protection. Every durability setting is a decision about how many to do.

cards.q: What was fsyncgate and what did Postgres change?
cards.a: In 2018 it emerged that on Linux, when writeback fails, the error is reported to the next fsync caller and the pages are then marked clean — so a retry returns success while the data is gone. Postgres 12 now panics on fsync failure and recovers from the WAL. The general lesson: an I/O error is not retryable unless you know what the layer beneath did with the failed data.

cards.q: What is a torn page, and what is Postgres's defence?
cards.a: A power cut partway through writing an 8 KB page leaves half new and half old, because hardware only guarantees atomicity at sector granularity. full_page_writes writes the entire page image into the WAL on its first modification after each checkpoint — roughly doubling WAL volume, and the reason disabling it is tempting and wrong.

cards.q: Derive the write-ahead log from first principles.
cards.a: Modifying a row means a random write, possibly across several pages, which cannot be made atomic. So append a description of the change to a sequential log, fsync it, and report the commit; update the data pages lazily later; replay the log after a crash. One random write becomes one sequential append plus one fsync.

cards.q: What does synchronous_commit = off actually risk?
cards.a: Not corruption — only the loss of the last fraction of a second of committed transactions. A reasonable trade for analytics ingestion or event logging and a bad one for payments. Also note group commit: concurrent commits share one fsync, so throughput scales far better than single-transaction latency suggests.

cards.q: What do innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit 1, 2 and 0 mean?
cards.a: 1 flushes per commit (durable, default); 2 writes to the page cache per commit and flushes each second, so it survives a process crash but not a power cut; 0 does neither.

cards.q: Which three iostat and top numbers diagnose storage, and what does each mean?
cards.a: await — average request latency, the number that matters. aqu-sz — queue depth; high await with a deep queue means saturation. %util — misleading on parallel-queue devices. And wa in top: high wa with low user CPU means the machine is storage-bound.

cards.q: Why did a database that was fast for three weeks become permanently slow?
cards.a: Exhausted burst credits on a burstable cloud volume (or a burstable instance). It drops to a baseline that can be a fraction of what you tested against, and no query tuning fixes it.

cards.q: Why must a database never run on a container's writable layer?
cards.a: Every first write to a file pays a full copy-up through the overlay driver. Volumes go to the host filesystem directly. It is a mechanical cost, not just a persistence concern.

cards.q: What does a filesystem lay out on a device?
cards.a: A superblock (size, block size, where everything is, a clean/dirty flag); allocation structures for free blocks and inodes; the inode table; and the data blocks.

cards.q: Why did extents replace indirect blocks?
cards.a: Indirect blocks describe a large file with hundreds of thousands of pointers. An extent is a start block plus a length, so a contiguous 1 GB file needs a handful of records. It is a large part of why ext4 outperforms ext3 on big files.

cards.q: Why is fsck unacceptable on a server, and what replaced it?
cards.a: Scanning a multi-terabyte filesystem takes hours during which the machine is down. Journaling replaced it: write a description of the intended updates to a journal and flush, perform them, mark the entry complete, and after a crash replay only the incomplete entries — bounded work in seconds.

cards.q: What do ext4's three data modes guarantee?
cards.a: data=journal: data and metadata both journaled, safest, everything written twice. data=ordered (default): metadata journaled, but data blocks forced to disk before the metadata referencing them, so you never see another file's old contents. data=writeback: no ordering, fastest, and after a crash a file can contain arbitrary stale bytes.

cards.q: Why can a crash leave a file that exists, has the right size, and is full of zeros?
cards.a: ext4 journals metadata, not data, and uses delayed allocation. It is documented behaviour of data=ordered, not a bug — which is why applications that care must fsync.

cards.q: Write a genuinely safe file update.
cards.a: Write the temp file; fsync the temp file; rename over the target; fsync the containing directory. The rename alone gives atomicity for readers but not durability against power loss.

cards.q: What is tmpfs and what is its container trap?
cards.a: A filesystem in RAM backed by the page cache and swap — /dev/shm, much of /run, Docker's --tmpfs, and Kubernetes' memory-medium emptyDir. Its contents count against your cgroup memory limit, so writing a few gigabytes into one gets the container OOMKilled for reasons the error does not explain.

cards.q: Why should a database never live on NFS?
cards.a: Network filesystems break local assumptions: locking is advisory and unreliable, fsync semantics vary, latency is milliseconds, and an unresponsive server puts your process into unkillable D state.

cards.q: Describe overlayfs's three operations.
cards.a: Read: search the upper layer, then each lower layer in order, first hit wins. Write to a lower-layer file: copy-up the entire file into the upper layer first, then modify. Delete a lower-layer file: create a whiteout marker in the upper layer to hide it.

cards.q: Explain layer sharing and why ten containers from one image are cheap.
cards.a: The lower directories are one set of files on disk, mounted read-only into every container; each container adds only a thin writable upper layer. It is also why a common base image across services is a real saving.

cards.q: Why does RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* in a separate instruction not shrink the image?
cards.a: The earlier layer still contains the files; the later layer only adds whiteouts. This is also how credentials leak: a secret deleted in a later instruction is still extractable from the layer where it was added. Hence multi-stage builds and BuildKit --mount=type=secret.

cards.q: Why is COPY package*.json then RUN npm ci then COPY . . not a style convention?
cards.a: A layer's cache is invalidated when its inputs change, and every layer after it is then rebuilt. This order puts the slow, rarely-invalidated step above the fast, always-invalidated one. Reversed, dependencies reinstall on every source change.

cards.q: Why is a bind mount slow on Docker Desktop?
cards.a: Linux containers there run inside a virtual machine, so the mount crosses from the host filesystem into the VM through a protocol (osxfs, then gRPC-FUSE, now VirtioFS). Every stat crosses it, and a bundler statting a hundred thousand files becomes an order of magnitude slower. Keep node_modules in a named volume, and on Windows work inside the WSL2 filesystem rather than /mnt/c.

cards.q: Why does import Button from './button' work on a Mac and fail in CI?
cards.a: APFS is case-insensitive by default; ext4 is case-sensitive. It is one of the most common works-on-my-machine failures in JavaScript projects and it is one line of filesystem behaviour.

cards.q: What is a user, to the kernel?
cards.a: An unsigned integer in the process's credentials. Usernames exist only in /etc/passwd, read by ordinary library code in user space to render numbers as names.

cards.q: Why does a container writing to a bind mount produce confusing ownership?
cards.a: UID 1000 inside and UID 1000 on the host are the same user to the kernel, regardless of what either side's /etc/passwd calls it — unless a user namespace maps them.

cards.q: How does the permission check pick which bits apply?
cards.a: First match wins: if you are the owner, only the owner bits apply, even if the group bits would grant more. A file you own with mode 044 is one you cannot read and everyone else can.

cards.q: What do r, w and x mean on a directory?
cards.a: r lists the names; w creates, deletes and renames entries — which is why deleting a file is governed by the directory's permissions, not the file's; x is search, permitting traversal to something inside. x without r lets you open a file whose exact name you know while preventing listing.

cards.q: What are setuid, setgid and the sticky bit?
cards.a: setuid runs a program as the file's owner — how passwd edits /etc/shadow, and a permanent source of privilege escalation. setgid does the same for groups and makes directory contents inherit the group. The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion to each file's owner, which is why /tmp is 1777.

cards.q: What is umask and why does it surprise people?
cards.a: A mask of bits removed from the mode of newly created files — the common 022 turns a requested 666 into 644. It is per-process state inherited by children, so a daemon's umask can differ from your shell's.

cards.q: Why do capabilities exist, and name five.
cards.a: Because all-or-nothing root means a server that needs to bind port 80 must start as root, leaving a window in which any bug is total compromise. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_NET_RAW (why ping often fails in a container), CAP_SYS_PTRACE, and CAP_SYS_ADMIN — a grab-bag including mount, widely called the new root.

cards.q: What does SELinux add beyond permission bits, and where do you meet it?
cards.a: Mandatory access control: a policy enforced regardless of ordinary permissions and not overridable by the file's owner. You meet it as the :z/:Z volume mount suffixes on Red Hat systems, where the failure without them is a permission denied the bits say should have worked.

cards.q: Justify each field of a hardened Kubernetes securityContext.
cards.a: runAsNonRoot/runAsUser: not UID 0, so an escape is not host root. allowPrivilegeEscalation: false: sets no_new_privs so setuid binaries cannot elevate. readOnlyRootFilesystem: with an emptyDir where writes are genuinely needed. capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}. seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault. Each is one mechanism from this document, turned off.

cards.q: Why do Node apps listen on 3000 or 8080?
cards.a: Ports below 1024 historically required root, so the pattern is a high port as a non-root user with nginx, a load balancer or a Service handling 80 and 443. You can also lower net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start, and Kubernetes generally sidesteps it.

cards.q: What are the three correct fixes for volume ownership mismatch?
cards.a: Match the UIDs deliberately (build the image with the host user's UID); use a named volume rather than a bind mount so the runtime handles ownership; or in Kubernetes set fsGroup. The genuinely correct answer is user namespaces. chmod 777, running as root, and chowning on startup are all bad.

cards.q: Why might fs.writeFile(path, data, {mode: 0o600}) not give you what you asked for?
cards.a: The mode is subject to umask. Writing a secret or a private key needs an explicit fs.chmod after creation or verification — and ssh silently rejects a group-readable private key, which is a habit worth copying.

cards.q: State the namespace mechanism in one sentence.
cards.a: Every global resource the kernel names becomes a per-process pointer to a table, so processes sharing a pointer see the same table and processes with different pointers see different ones.

cards.q: Why is a namespace not a restriction?
cards.a: It changes what exists as far as that process is concerned. A process in its own PID namespace does not fail to kill PID 4321; there is no PID 4321 in its numbering. Isolation by construction rather than by check — which is why it is cheap and complete for what it covers.

cards.q: Name the seven namespaces and what each virtualises.
cards.a: Mount (the mount tree, 2002); PID (the process ID space, 2008); Network (interfaces, routes, firewall rules and the port space, 2009); UTS (hostname, 2006); IPC (System V and POSIX message queues, semaphores, shared memory, 2006); User (UID/GID mapping, completed 2013); Cgroup (position in the cgroup hierarchy, 2016).

cards.q: Why can two containers both bind port 3000?
cards.a: The network namespace has a private port number space. It is the most visible benefit of namespaces and it follows from one sentence.

cards.q: How is a container connected to a network at all?
cards.a: A veth pair — a virtual cable — with one end inside the namespace and the other attached to a host bridge (docker0), plus iptables NAT rules for published ports.

cards.q: Why is the user namespace the most consequential one?
cards.a: It maps UIDs to the parent's, so a process can be root in its namespace with no privilege on the host — the correct solution to volume ownership and the basis of rootless containers. It is also the only namespace an unprivileged user may create, and for that reason a recurring source of kernel privilege-escalation vulnerabilities.

cards.q: Name the three system calls that operate on namespaces and what each is used for.
cards.a: clone() with CLONE_NEW* flags creates a process in new namespaces (container creation); unshare() moves the caller into new ones; setns() joins an existing one given a descriptor — which is what docker exec and kubectl exec do.

cards.q: What is not namespaced, and why does each matter?
cards.a: The kernel itself (so a kernel bug affects every container and a panic takes them all down — the fundamental difference from a VM); the system clock; most of /proc/sys; and the CPU count and memory totals reported by /proc — which is why os.cpus().length, nproc and lscpu all lie inside a container.

cards.q: Define a Kubernetes pod precisely, and derive four of its behaviours.
cards.a: Containers sharing the network and IPC namespaces and usually UTS, with separate mount and PID namespaces. Hence: localhost between them; they cannot both bind 8080; no shared files without a shared volume; and no visibility of each other's processes without shareProcessNamespace.

cards.q: What is the pause container for?
cards.a: It holds the pod's network namespace and does nothing but sleep, so the namespace survives individual containers restarting.

cards.q: How does a service mesh sidecar intercept traffic without the application knowing?
cards.a: It is in the same network namespace, and iptables rules redirect the application's traffic through it. The application needs no awareness at all.

cards.q: What do Docker's host and none network modes mean mechanically?
cards.a: host means not creating a network namespace — the container shares the host's, so there is no NAT, no port mapping, full performance and no isolation. none creates an empty one.

cards.q: What is a cgroup and how do you configure one?
cards.a: A set of processes plus resource controllers, arranged in a hierarchy exposed as a filesystem — so configuring limits is writing text into files under /sys/fs/cgroup. Google, 2006 (as process containers), merged in Linux 2.6.24 in 2008.

cards.q: Distinguish cpu.weight from cpu.max.
cards.a: cpu.weight is a relative share (1–10000, default 100), CFS's task weight applied to a group — it only matters under contention, and an uncontended group gets everything. cpu.max is a hard quota written as quota and period: at most N µs per period, after which every task in the group is stopped until the next period, even on an idle machine.

cards.q: Do the throttling arithmetic for a one-core limit and five busy threads.
cards.a: The 100 ms quota is consumed in 20 ms of wall clock, then the container sleeps for 80 ms. Average utilisation reads as 100% of one core, and every request arriving in those 80 ms takes an extra 80 ms. That is latency spikes at apparently fine CPU.

cards.q: State the argument for requests without CPU limits, and the counter-argument.
cards.a: Requests give a guaranteed share under contention; limits only add throttling and cannot make anything faster, so for latency-sensitive services limits are pure cost. The counter-argument is that without them a misbehaving container degrades its neighbours. Both are defensible; the decision should be made knowingly.

cards.q: Name the three memory thresholds and say which Kubernetes exposes.
cards.a: memory.max — hard; exceeding it triggers reclaim and then the cgroup OOM killer. memory.high — soft; above it the kernel throttles allocations and reclaims hard, making the group slow rather than dead. memory.min/low — reclaim protection. Kubernetes exposes only the hard one, which is a genuine gap.

cards.q: What does pids.max defend against?
cards.a: A fork bomb. Without it one container can exhaust the machine's PID space and nothing anywhere can start a process.

cards.q: What is PSI and why is it a better signal than utilisation?
cards.a: Pressure Stall Information (Linux 4.20, 2018) reports the fraction of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory or I/O. Utilisation says how busy something is; pressure says how much your work is being delayed, which is what you actually care about. It is what modern autoscaling and oomd use.

cards.q: Map Kubernetes resource fields to cgroup files.
cards.a: requests.cpu → cpu.weight; limits.cpu → cpu.max (throttling); requests.memory → scheduling and reclaim protection; limits.memory → memory.max (OOM kill).

cards.q: State the asymmetry between CPU and memory limits and explain why it exists.
cards.a: Exceeding a CPU limit makes you slow; exceeding a memory limit makes you dead. CPU is compressible — give a process less and it still runs. Memory is not: there is nothing to give back once the bytes are written.

cards.q: What are the QoS classes and what do they determine?
cards.a: Guaranteed (requests equal limits everywhere), Burstable, and BestEffort (nothing set, oom_score_adj 1000). They determine who the kernel kills first when the node runs out of memory — so setting requests is a survival decision, not just a scheduling hint.

cards.q: How does systemd give you container-style limits with no container?
cards.a: It puts every service in its own cgroup, so MemoryMax=, CPUQuota= and TasksMax= in a unit file are exactly these mechanisms. systemd-cgtop shows resource use by cgroup.

cards.q: Define a container in one sentence.
cards.a: An ordinary Linux process — visible in the host's process list with a real PID — started with a particular combination of namespaces, cgroups, a layered root filesystem, a credential mapping, a capability set and a syscall filter. The kernel has no container object.

cards.q: What are the three parts of an OCI image?
cards.a: Layers (tar archives of filesystem differences, content-addressed); a config (default command, environment, user, and the ordered layer digests); and a manifest listing both, whose own digest is the image's digest. A manifest list maps architectures to manifests.

cards.q: Why should production reference image@sha256:... rather than a tag?
cards.a: Digests are immutable; tags are mutable pointers. It is also why imagePullPolicy: Always exists.

cards.q: Walk the eleven steps of docker run.
cards.a: Resolve and pull; assemble the overlay filesystem; create the cgroup and write limits; clone() with namespace flags; wire the veth pair and NAT rules; pivot_root and unmount the old root; mount /proc, /sys, /dev; set the hostname; set UID, drop capabilities, set no_new_privs, install seccomp and the LSM label; set environment, working directory and stdio; execve the entrypoint.

cards.q: Why pivot_root rather than chroot?
cards.a: pivot_root unmounts the old root afterwards, so the host filesystem is no longer reachable at all. chroot is escapable.

cards.q: Place runc, containerd, the shim, Docker, Podman and BuildKit.
cards.a: runc performs the eleven steps from an OCI bundle. containerd manages images, storage, networking and lifecycle and calls runc; Kubernetes talks to it through the CRI. The shim is one small process per container so containerd can restart without killing containers and so someone collects exit statuses. Docker is a developer-facing layer over containerd. Podman is daemonless and rootless by default. BuildKit is the parallel, cache-mount and secret-mount capable builder.

cards.q: Why did removing Docker support from Kubernetes 1.24 change nothing about your images?
cards.a: containerd was underneath all along, and Docker-built images are OCI images.

cards.q: How do you debug a distroless container?
cards.a: nsenter -t <host-pid> -n -p -m from the host puts a shell into its namespaces with no tooling in the image; docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' gets the PID. In Kubernetes, kubectl debug creates an ephemeral container in the pod's namespaces.

cards.q: State a container's security properties honestly.
cards.a: Isolation rests entirely on kernel correctness, because there is one kernel and every container calls into it directly, so a reachable privilege-escalation bug is a host compromise. That is a different risk profile from a VM, and it is why untrusted multi-tenant workloads use gVisor, Kata or Firecracker. Mitigations by value: not root, drop all capabilities, seccomp, read-only root, user namespace.

cards.q: How old is virtualisation, and what question was it answering?
cards.a: IBM CP-40 and CP-67 from 1967, productised as VM/370 in 1972 and still sold as z/VM. Time-sharing and virtualisation were competing answers to the same question of how to share an expensive machine — one shares an operating system among users, the other gives each user a whole machine.

cards.q: What is the Popek–Goldberg requirement and why did x86 fail it?
cards.a: Every instruction that could reveal or change privileged state must trap when executed unprivileged. Seventeen x86 instructions behaved differently in user mode instead of trapping — popf silently ignoring interrupt-flag changes, for instance — so a guest kernel got wrong answers with no way for the hypervisor to notice.

cards.q: Name the three historical responses to that failure.
cards.a: Binary translation (VMware, 1999 — rewrite the guest's problematic instructions as it executes); paravirtualisation (Xen, 2003 — modify the guest to call the hypervisor explicitly); and hardware virtualisation (Intel VT-x and AMD-V, 2005 — a mode beneath ring 0, which made the cloud economically possible).

cards.q: What are second-level address translation and the IOMMU for?
cards.a: SLAT (EPT/NPT) lets the MMU walk both the guest's and the hypervisor's page tables in hardware, replacing expensive shadow page tables. The IOMMU translates the addresses a device uses for DMA, which is what makes it safe to hand a physical NIC or GPU directly to a guest.

cards.q: What is virtio and why does every cloud image boot anywhere?
cards.a: Rather than emulating a real device register by register — slow and pointless when the guest knows it is virtualised — virtio defines paravirtual devices with a shared ring-buffer interface. Every Linux guest has the drivers built in.

cards.q: Compare containers and VMs on six axes.
cards.a: Kernel: shared vs its own. Isolation: kernel correctness vs hardware. Start: milliseconds (a clone()) vs seconds (a full boot). Overhead: a process vs a kernel and its memory. Density: hundreds vs tens. Guest OS: must match the host kernel vs anything. Plus: live migration is mature for VMs and essentially absent for containers.

cards.q: What is Firecracker and why does it exist?
cards.a: A minimal KVM-based VMM from AWS (2018, in Rust) emulating five devices, booting a microVM in ~125 ms with ~5 MB overhead. It exists because AWS needed hardware-level isolation between customers' functions with container-like start times. It runs Lambda and Fargate.

cards.q: Why is the usual production answer both containers and VMs?
cards.a: Your Kubernetes nodes are cloud instances: the VM boundary separates tenants, and the container boundary separates your own workloads and gives packaging and density. Presenting it as a choice usually indicates not having run multi-tenant infrastructure.

cards.q: Explain four Docker Desktop frustrations with one fact.
cards.a: Containers run inside a Linux VM because macOS and Windows lack the kernel features. Hence: the memory figure is the VM's allocation; bind mounts cross a filesystem boundary and are slow; --network host means the VM's network, not your Mac's; and host.docker.internal exists to reach the host.

cards.q: What changed between WSL1 and WSL2, and what does it mean for file performance?
cards.a: WSL1 translated Linux syscalls into NT kernel calls — a compatibility layer, fast on Windows files, incomplete, and unable to run Docker. WSL2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight VM, so it is fully compatible, and the filesystem story inverts: files under the Linux root are fast, /mnt/c crosses the boundary. Moving a project inside WSL2 is often a five-to-tenfold build improvement.

cards.q: Explain a serverless cold start mechanically, and which optimisations follow.
cards.a: Booting a microVM plus initialising the runtime plus demand-paging your code. So smaller packages help (less to fault in), provisioned concurrency keeps the VM warm, SnapStart replaces the boot with a restore, and raising memory also raises CPU — which is why a CPU-bound function can be cheaper at a higher memory setting.

cards.q: What is a signal and how is it delivered?
cards.a: A software interrupt: a small integer with no payload. The kernel sets a bit in the target's pending mask; when that process is next about to return to user mode, the kernel applies the default action or arranges the stack so it resumes inside the handler. So a signal is delivered when the process next runs, not when it is sent.

cards.q: Give the numbers and meanings of the eight signals that matter.
cards.a: 1 SIGHUP (terminal gone; reused as reload); 2 SIGINT (Ctrl-C); 9 SIGKILL (uncatchable); 11 SIGSEGV; 13 SIGPIPE; 15 SIGTERM (the polite request, kill's default); 17 SIGCHLD; 19/18 SIGSTOP/SIGCONT.

cards.q: Why is there no such thing as cleanup on SIGKILL?
cards.a: It cannot be caught, blocked or ignored — deliberately, so there is always a way to stop a process that refuses to cooperate. No flush, no close, no final log line. Which is why every graceful shutdown design must live on SIGTERM, and why an OOM kill gives you nothing.

cards.q: Why may a signal handler not call malloc?
cards.a: It runs at an arbitrary point, possibly inside malloc holding the allocator's lock, so calling it deadlocks against the interrupted code. POSIX defines a short list of async-signal-safe functions; printf and malloc are not on it.

cards.q: What is the self-pipe trick, and why is your Node SIGTERM handler unrestricted?
cards.a: The handler writes one byte to a pipe and returns; the main loop reads it as an ordinary event. Linux later added signalfd. libuv does exactly this, so by the time your JavaScript callback runs it is a normal event-loop callback, not a signal handler.

cards.q: Why must a SIGCHLD handler reap in a loop?
cards.a: Standard signals do not queue — the pending set is a bitmask, so ten SIGCHLDs while one is blocked leave one bit. while (waitpid(-1, &st, WNOHANG) > 0);.

cards.q: What are PID 1's two special kernel behaviours?
cards.a: Signals with default actions are not delivered to it — the kernel refuses, so an unhandled SIGTERM is silently discarded. And it inherits orphans and is expected to reap them.

cards.q: Why does your container appear to take ten seconds to stop?
cards.a: docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits ten seconds, then SIGKILLs. Node as PID 1 with no handler discards the first signal entirely. It is not slowness — the polite request was thrown away.

cards.q: Why does CMD npm start break shutdown?
cards.a: It runs sh -c "npm start", so a shell is PID 1 and does not forward signals to its child. Your Node process never hears about the shutdown. ENTRYPOINT ["node", "server.js"] — exec form — fixes it, and this is the most common Dockerfile defect in the wild.

cards.q: Why is the ordering in a Kubernetes graceful shutdown a race, and what is the fix?
cards.a: When a pod is deleted, SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen concurrently, and the removal takes time to propagate through kube-proxy on every node. Stopping accept immediately refuses traffic still being routed to you — a burst of 502s on every deploy. Delay the actual shutdown a few seconds, or use a preStop sleep.

cards.q: Write the shape of a correct Node graceful shutdown.
cards.a: Fail readiness first and wait for the load balancer's probe period; then server.close() and closeIdleConnections(); then drain workers and the database pool; and set a hard process.exit deadline below terminationGracePeriodSeconds so you always exit on your own terms rather than being SIGKILLed.

cards.q: Why does Node give you EPIPE rather than SIGPIPE?
cards.a: Node ignores SIGPIPE and surfaces the condition as a stream error, which is why writing to a socket the client already closed emits 'error' — and why an unhandled 'error' listener crashes the process. A client navigating away mid-response is normal traffic, not a fault.

cards.q: What is SIGUSR1 used for in Node, and why is that useful in production?
cards.a: It opens the debugger port, which is a genuinely useful way to attach a profiler to a running production process without restarting it.

cards.q: Why is reaching for kill -9 first a habit worth losing?
cards.a: It skips every cleanup path the program has. If SIGTERM did not work the reason is worth knowing — usually a missing handler, a shell as PID 1, or a D-state hang that -9 will not fix either.

cards.q: What three things does every IPC mechanism trade?
cards.a: Speed, whether the parties must be related, and whether it works across machines.

cards.q: What can a Unix domain socket do that a TCP socket cannot?
cards.a: Pass file descriptors (SCM_RIGHTS) — transferring an open descriptor to another process, where it becomes a new number referring to the same open file description — and report verified peer credentials (SO_PEERCRED): the connecting process's real UID, GID and PID, checked by the kernel and unforgeable.

cards.q: Why is shared memory the fastest and also the most dangerous?
cards.a: The same physical frames appear in two address spaces, so there is no copy at all — and no synchronisation whatsoever, so you must supply your own atomics or locks, and a bug is a data race across a process boundary.

cards.q: Give the default choice for local IPC and justify it.
cards.a: Unix domain sockets: as fast as anything that copies, the same API as networking so code ports trivially, and they carry descriptors and credentials. Reach for shared memory only when profiling proves the copy is the bottleneck.

cards.q: What does child.send(obj) cost, and what is it wrong for?
cards.a: Serialisation plus two copies plus two syscalls over a Unix socket pair — cheap for coordination, completely wrong for a shared cache. The listening socket, by contrast, is passed once as a descriptor via SCM_RIGHTS.

cards.q: Why is worker_threads messaging not IPC?
cards.a: Workers are threads in one process, so postMessage is an in-memory structured clone with no kernel involvement — no syscall, no socket. transferList avoids even the copy, and SharedArrayBuffer is shared memory with Atomics as the synchronisation.

cards.q: What do you gain by pointing nginx at a Unix socket instead of loopback TCP?
cards.a: No handshake, no ephemeral port allocation, no TIME_WAIT accumulation, and lower latency — plus the service becomes unreachable from the network by construction. The same applies to Postgres, whose local lines in pg_hba.conf use peer authentication via SO_PEERCRED.

cards.q: Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container a host compromise?
cards.a: The daemon authorises by peer credentials, so anything that can talk to it can start a privileged container, mount the host filesystem, and read every secret on the machine. Alternatives: a rootless daemon, a socket proxy whitelisting specific API calls, or a daemonless builder like Kaniko or rootless BuildKit.

cards.q: Explain Redis's architectural role as a consequence of Node 5.
cards.a: Separate processes have separate address spaces, so once you have cluster workers or replicas across machines, nothing local works between them. Rate limiter counters, session stores, cache, pub/sub for websocket fan-out and BullMQ queues are one problem — state visible to processes with separate address spaces — solved by a process everyone can reach over a socket.

cards.q: Why does the socket API use file descriptors?
cards.a: 4.2BSD, 1983, Berkeley: reusing the descriptor meant network endpoints could be read and written like anything else — Node 21's uniform interface paying off again.

cards.q: What identifies a TCP connection, and why does that matter?
cards.a: The four-tuple: source address, source port, destination address, destination port. The kernel hashes it to route an incoming packet to the right socket, and it is what bounds ephemeral port exhaustion.

cards.q: Name the two backlog queues and what each fills from.
cards.a: The SYN queue holds half-open connections awaiting the final ACK (tcp_max_syn_backlog; SYN floods target it, and SYN cookies defend by encoding state into the sequence number). The accept queue holds established connections waiting for your program to call accept() (the listen() backlog, capped by somaxconn) — it fills when your process is not accepting fast enough.

cards.q: How do you detect a blocked event loop from the network side?
cards.a: ss -lnt shows Recv-Q as the current accept-queue depth against Send-Q as its limit, and nstat -az TcpExtListenOverflows counts drops. Rising overflows with healthy CPU is one of the cleanest possible diagnoses.

cards.q: Distinguish flow control from congestion control.
cards.a: Flow control protects the receiver: every ACK carries a receive window and the sender may not exceed it — TCP-level backpressure. Congestion control protects the network: the sender grows a congestion window on success and shrinks it on loss.

cards.q: Why does the first ~14 KB of a response arrive faster than the rest?
cards.a: Slow start begins with about ten packets and doubles each round trip, so a larger response takes several round trips to ramp. That is where the advice about keeping critical CSS under 14 KB came from.

cards.q: What does BBR do differently from CUBIC?
cards.a: CUBIC treats loss as the congestion signal — grow, halve on loss. BBR models the path's bandwidth and round-trip time directly, so it performs far better on links that drop packets for reasons other than congestion: mobile and long-distance. Enabling it on an edge server sometimes produces a startling improvement.

cards.q: What is bandwidth-delay product and when does it cap you?
cards.a: A 100 ms round trip at 1 Gbps needs about 12 MB in flight to keep the pipe full; if the receive buffer is smaller, throughput is capped by latency regardless of available bandwidth. Hence buffer autotuning and slow long-distance transfers.

cards.q: Give the two real reasons for TIME_WAIT.
cards.a: A delayed duplicate packet from this connection must not be delivered to a new connection reusing the same four-tuple; and if the final ACK is lost, the peer retransmits its FIN and someone must answer. It lasts 60 seconds on Linux and is not tunable without recompiling.

cards.q: Why does a client opening ~500 connections per second to one destination start failing?
cards.a: The side that closes first accumulates TIME_WAIT sockets for a minute each, and the ephemeral port range is about 28,000 ports — so it exhausts them and gets EADDRNOTAVAIL. The real fix is keep-alive and pooling, not tuning.

cards.q: Distinguish SO_REUSEADDR from SO_REUSEPORT.
cards.a: SO_REUSEADDR lets a server bind a port that has connections in TIME_WAIT — without it, restarting fails with EADDRINUSE for a minute, which is why every framework sets it. SO_REUSEPORT (Linux 3.9, 2013) lets several processes bind the same port with the kernel load-balancing between them, which is what nginx workers use.

cards.q: Decode ECONNREFUSED, ETIMEDOUT, ECONNRESET and EPIPE.
cards.a: Refused: the destination sent RST — reachable, nothing listening; fast and definitive. Timed out on connect: no reply at all — a firewall dropping silently or a wrong address. Reset: the peer sent RST on an established connection — it crashed, closed with unread data, a load balancer idle timeout, or a keep-alive socket reused as the server closed it. EPIPE: you wrote to a connection the peer has closed.

cards.q: Why does ECONNRESET appear intermittently on a pooled HTTP client, and what fixes it?
cards.a: A race: your agent picks a pooled socket the server is simultaneously closing. Keep the client's idle timeout below the server's, and retry idempotent requests on it.

cards.q: Why is keepAlive: true the single highest-value line in a Lambda calling other services?
cards.a: A new HTTPS connection costs a TCP round trip, a TLS round trip and slow start; reuse costs nothing. Node's http.Agent defaulted to keepAlive: false until Node 19, and a function instance handles many invocations.

cards.q: What is a Kubernetes Service, mechanically, and what does that break?
cards.a: Packet rewriting, not a proxy: kube-proxy programs netfilter (iptables, IPVS, or eBPF) so a packet to the Service IP has its destination rewritten to a chosen pod IP, on the sending node. Load balancing is per connection, so a long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connection pins to one pod forever — which is why gRPC clients and meshes need explicit balancing.

cards.q: What causes intermittent connection failures across every workload on one node with all applications healthy?
cards.a: The nf_conntrack table is full — NAT and stateful firewalling require remembering every connection, and when the table fills new connections are dropped with a kernel log line. Check conntrack -C against nf_conntrack_max.

cards.q: Explain head-of-line blocking at three layers and how HTTP evolved past each.
cards.a: HTTP/1.1 blocks at the request layer (hence six connections per host). HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one connection, removing it at the HTTP layer — but not at TCP's, where one lost packet stalls every stream. HTTP/3 abandons TCP for QUIC over UDP, doing reliability per stream in user space, and merges the transport and TLS handshakes.

cards.q: What is a PMTU black hole and what is its signature?
cards.a: Overlay networks and VPNs add encapsulation, lowering the effective MTU; when a firewall blocks the ICMP fragmentation-needed message, path MTU discovery fails silently. Signature: small requests succeed and large POST bodies hang forever on the same connection path.

cards.q: Why is DNS slow inside a Kubernetes pod, and what are the fixes?
cards.a: The default ndots: 5 means any name with fewer than five dots is tried against every search domain first — four or five failing queries, for both A and AAAA. Fixes: a trailing dot, an explicit dnsConfig with lower ndots, or NodeLocal DNSCache. And dns.lookup uses the threadpool, so slow DNS also blocks file I/O.

cards.q: Name the four compilation stages and attribute one error to each.
cards.a: Preprocessing (a missing header); compiling (a syntax or type error); assembling; linking (undefined reference to ...). They are separate programs, which is why each fails with its own kind of error.

cards.q: What is in an object file besides machine code?
cards.a: A symbol table — names this file defines with their offsets, and names it references but does not define — and relocations, a list of positions containing placeholders plus instructions for patching each once the real address is known.

cards.q: What are the linker's two jobs and its two failure modes?
cards.a: Symbol resolution (find a definition for every undefined symbol) and relocation (assign final addresses and patch every placeholder). It fails with undefined reference or multiple definition.

cards.q: Why does link order matter in C?
cards.a: A static library is an archive of object files, and the linker pulls out only members resolving something still undefined. A library listed before the code that uses it contributes nothing.

cards.q: What are ELF's two views of the same bytes?
cards.a: Section headers — the linker's fine-grained view (.text, .rodata, .data, .bss, .symtab, debug info). Program headers — the loader's coarse view: a handful of segments, each a region to mmap with given permissions, which is the direct input to the address space layout.

cards.q: Why does a program with a 100 MB zeroed global array produce a small file?
cards.a: .bss occupies no space in the file — only a size. The pages are allocated and zeroed at load time.

cards.q: Why does file report a modern executable as a shared object?
cards.a: It is ET_DYN — position-independent, loadable at any address, which is what ASLR requires. Essentially all modern binaries are built as position-independent executables.

cards.q: Map eight linker concepts onto bundler concepts.
cards.a: Object file → module; undefined symbol → import; defined symbol → export; symbol resolution → module resolution; undefined reference → Module not found; multiple definition → two copies of React; dead code elimination → tree shaking; stripping → minification; DWARF → source maps; shared library → code splitting and import().

cards.q: Why can ES modules be tree-shaken and CommonJS largely not?
cards.a: Dead-code elimination requires static references — require(someVariable) is unresolvable at build time, exactly as a function pointer defeats a linker's reachability analysis.

cards.q: What are you promising with "sideEffects": false?
cards.a: That importing a module purely for its side effects never happens, which lets the bundler drop unreferenced modules entirely — the same promise --gc-sections relies on.

cards.q: Why does two copies of React give a hooks error rather than a duplication error?
cards.a: It is a multiple-definition problem that the JavaScript module system does not report as an error. You silently get two module instances with two separate pieces of internal state.

cards.q: Explain three .node addon failure modes from this node.
cards.a: Architecture-specific machine code (invalid ELF header when built on a Mac and run in a linux/amd64 container); ABI-specific (NODE_MODULE_VERSION mismatch, which N-API fixes with a stable ABI); and needing a compiler at install time unless prebuilt binaries are shipped, which is what prebuild-install and node-pre-gyp do.

cards.q: Why can a project type-check cleanly and still fail at run time with module-not-found?
cards.a: tsc performs the compile stages per file and there is no linker; module resolution happens at run time or bundle time, by a different tool with different rules. tsc's paths being satisfied does not mean the runtime resolver agrees.

cards.q: What does dynamic linking defer, and who does it?
cards.a: Symbol resolution and relocation, to run time, performed by the dynamic linker named in the executable's PT_INTERP segment — /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 on Linux — before the program's first instruction.

cards.q: State dynamic linking's three benefits and three costs.
cards.a: Benefits: one copy of libc shared in memory by every process; a library security fix takes effect everywhere on next start; smaller executables. Costs: startup does work that used to be build-time; the deployment environment must supply compatible libraries; version mismatches become run-time failures.

cards.q: How do the PLT and GOT implement lazy binding?
cards.a: A call jumps to a PLT stub, which reads an address from the GOT and jumps there. Initially the GOT entry points back into the linker, so the first call triggers resolution, which writes the real address into the GOT; subsequent calls go straight through.

cards.q: What is RELRO and what does it trade?
cards.a: Resolving everything eagerly at startup and marking the GOT read-only, so an attacker cannot overwrite an entry to redirect a call. LD_BIND_NOW=1 or -z now. Slightly slower startup for a closed attack surface.

cards.q: What causes cannot open shared object file, and how do you diagnose it?
cards.a: The library was not found on the search path (RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, RUNPATH, the ldconfig cache, defaults). ldd <binary> lists what it needs and where each was found; not found lines are the answer.

cards.q: What is LD_PRELOAD and give one good and one bad use.
cards.a: A list of libraries loaded before all others, so their symbols win — letting you replace any library function in any program with no recompilation. Good: swapping in jemalloc with one environment variable, or injecting tracing. Bad: a classic attacker persistence technique, which is why it is ignored for setuid binaries.

cards.q: State glibc's compatibility asymmetry and the rule it implies.
cards.a: Backward compatible, not forward compatible: a binary built against 2.31 runs on 2.36, but one built against 2.36 fails on 2.31 with version 'GLIBC_2.34' not found. So build on the oldest system you must support — which is why release pipelines pin an old base image.

cards.q: Name four real differences between Alpine and a glibc image.
cards.a: Binaries are not interchangeable, so prebuilt native modules often fall back to compiling from source; DNS resolution differs (no NSS, parallel A/AAAA on one socket) producing intermittent failures; musl's allocator is slower under multi-threaded allocation-heavy load; and the default thread stack is 128 KB rather than 8 MB.

cards.q: Give a defensible default among alpine, slim and distroless for a Node service.
cards.a: node:20-slim — Debian-based, glibc, ~75 MB — is the safer default. Alpine is worth it when image size genuinely matters and you have tested your dependency tree. Distroless gives glibc with no shell or package manager and the smallest attack surface, at the cost of needing ephemeral containers to debug.

cards.q: Why can a Go binary run in a FROM scratch image?
cards.a: It is statically linked and issues syscalls directly, so it depends on nothing but the kernel's permanent ABI. Rust with the musl target does the same. Node cannot — it is a large C++ program with a dynamic-linking-dependent addon system.

cards.q: In what sense is require() dynamic linking?
cards.a: It resolves a name to a file at run time, loads it, executes it, and caches it — symbol lookup, mapping, initialisation and a load cache. require.cache is why a module executes once, exactly as a shared object initialises once. And nested node_modules lets two versions coexist, which the ELF linker cannot easily do.

cards.q: Give the two independent reasons host node_modules must never be copied into an image.
cards.a: The native addons were compiled for your host's architecture (Node 33) and against your host's libc (Node 34). The errors — invalid ELF header and a missing shared object or symbol version — do not obviously say so. .dockerignore containing node_modules is a correctness requirement, not a size optimisation.

cards.q: What does execve change and what does it keep?
cards.a: It replaces the program: the address space is destroyed and rebuilt. The PID, the parent, open descriptors (except close-on-exec), and credentials are kept. It creates no process.

cards.q: How does a shebang work, and who handles it?
cards.a: The kernel, not the shell: on seeing #! it reads the interpreter path and re-runs execve on the interpreter with the script as an argument. The path must be absolute, which is why #!/usr/bin/env node is used, and only one argument is portably allowed after it.

cards.q: Why do signal handlers reset at exec but the signal mask does not?
cards.a: The handler code no longer exists, so handlers must reset to default. The mask is inherited — a genuine trap, since a process that blocked a signal and then execs passes the block to the new program, and services have failed to receive SIGTERM for exactly this reason.

cards.q: When does execve return?
cards.a: Only on failure. On success there is nothing to return to, because the calling code no longer exists.

cards.q: What is an environment variable, precisely?
cards.a: Per-process memory: an array of KEY=VALUE strings copied onto the new stack at exec, with no kernel involvement afterwards.

cards.q: Derive four environment-variable behaviours from that definition.
cards.a: A child cannot modify its parent's (no channel exists); changing one after a process starts does not affect it (hence restarting a service); process.env.FOO = 'x' affects only children spawned afterwards; and they are visible in /proc/<pid>/environ and ps eww, which is why they are a poor place for secrets.

cards.q: Why is ENOENT from spawn misleading?
cards.a: It means the program was not found, not your file argument. PATH is searched by the shell or by execvp, not by the bare syscall — so a minimal PATH produces it.

cards.q: What does a shell do with ls -l | grep .js > out.txt?
cards.a: Tokenise and expand (globs, variables, command substitution — which is why rm *.txt is expanded before rm sees it); create a pipe; fork twice; wire descriptors with dup2; exec both; waitpid.

cards.q: What is a process group and why does Ctrl-C interrupt a whole pipeline?
cards.a: The shell puts each pipeline in its own process group and the terminal has a foreground group; Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to every process in it. A background process reading from the terminal gets SIGTTIN and stops.

cards.q: Describe npm start's process tree and its three consequences.
cards.a: Shell → npm (a Node process) → sh -c "node server.js" → node server.js. Signals do not reach the bottom; exit codes are relayed badly and npm's own error output obscures the real one; and node_modules/.bin is prepended to PATH, which is the whole mechanism by which "test": "jest" works.

cards.q: Why does one word — exec — decide whether a container shuts down gracefully?
cards.a: exec node server.js at the end of an entrypoint script replaces the shell, so Node becomes PID 1 and receives signals directly. Without it the shell stays as PID 1 with Node as its child, and shutdown breaks.

cards.q: When is child_process.exec a security vulnerability?
cards.a: Whenever any part of the command string comes from user input: it runs through a shell, which interprets ;, &&, backticks and $(). Use spawn with an argument array, where each argument is a separate argv entry and no shell is involved.

cards.q: What does allowPrivilegeEscalation: false do, and at which step?
cards.a: It sets no_new_privs so the kernel ignores setuid bits at execve — step one, the permission check. A near-zero-cost mitigation for a whole class of container escape.

cards.q: State the bootstrap problem and its resolution.
