cards.a: To load a program you need a program. The first program is not loaded at all — it is physically present in non-volatile memory at an address the processor is wired to start from (0xFFFFFFF0 on x86, where the chipset maps the firmware flash).

cards.q: How does BIOS boot, and what are its two crude constraints?
cards.a: It reads the first 512-byte sector of the boot device to 0x7C00, checks the 0x55AA signature, and jumps. That leaves 446 bytes for code after the partition table — hence multi-stage bootloaders. And it starts the processor in 16-bit real mode, compatible with the 1978 8086.

cards.q: What does UEFI change?
cards.a: It understands FAT32 so it reads files from an EFI System Partition rather than raw sectors; it starts in 32- or 64-bit mode; it has a boot manager with a variable store (efibootmgr); and it supports Secure Boot, verifying each stage's signature — which is why an unsigned kernel module fails to load.

cards.q: What is the initramfs for?
cards.a: A chicken-and-egg fix: the kernel must mount the root filesystem, but the drivers for the controller and filesystem may live on it. So a small archive is loaded into memory as a temporary root containing exactly the modules and tools needed — storage drivers, LVM, disk encryption (the passphrase prompt) — and discarded once the real root is mounted.

cards.q: What does the kernel do between decompression and PID 1?
cards.a: Set up early page tables and switch to virtual addressing; initialise the IDT; bring secondary cores out of halt; initialise the allocator, scheduler and timers; initialise built-in drivers; mount the initramfs; find and mount the real root; and exec /sbin/init.

cards.q: What is /proc/cmdline and name three things you might find there.
cards.a: The kernel command line assembled by the bootloader: root=UUID=..., plus options like transparent_hugepage=never, systemd.unified_cgroup_hierarchy=1, or mitigations=off.

cards.q: Why does a container start in milliseconds?
cards.a: Nothing in this node happens — no firmware, bootloader, kernel decompression, device initialisation, initramfs or init system. It is clone() plus execve() on a kernel that is already running.

cards.q: What is cloud-init and why is the metadata endpoint a security concern?
cards.a: An early service that fetches instance metadata from 169.254.169.254, sets the hostname, installs SSH keys, grows the root partition and runs your user-data. SSRF against that endpoint was the mechanism of the 2019 Capital One breach; IMDSv2's session-token requirement exists to make it harder.

cards.q: Why can a container require a newer kernel feature than it will get?
cards.a: Containers do not bring a kernel. Your Alpine container on an Ubuntu host uses the Ubuntu kernel, so cgroups v2, io_uring and newer seccomp actions all depend on the host — which is why node image versions are worth tracking.

cards.q: What are PID 1's four jobs?
cards.a: Start services respecting dependencies; supervise them and decide about restarts with backoff; reap orphans; and shut down cleanly in dependency order with a deadline.

cards.q: Name SysV init's four structural problems.
cards.a: Strictly sequential, since ordering was encoded as filename numbers; no real dependency model, only ordering; no supervision, so a crashed service stayed dead (hence daemontools, runit, supervisord, pm2); and no reliable process tracking, because a double-forking daemon detaches and PID files go stale.

cards.q: Why does separating Requires= from After= matter?
cards.a: Requirement and ordering become independent, so you can require without ordering and order without requiring — and everything not explicitly ordered can start in parallel, which is where the boot-time improvement came from.

cards.q: Why does systemd track services by cgroup?
cards.a: So it knows every process belonging to a service regardless of forking or daemonising — no PID files, no guessing — and systemctl stop can reliably kill the whole tree. It also makes MemoryMax=, CPUQuota= and TasksMax= available to any service.

cards.q: What is socket activation and what does it make less important?
cards.a: systemd creates the listening socket and passes the descriptor to the service when a connection arrives. Services can start on demand, and dependency ordering matters less because a client connecting to a not-yet-started service simply waits in the accept queue.

cards.q: Name the systemd directives that are Part VI mechanisms, and what each is.
cards.a: PrivateTmp=true is a mount namespace; ProtectSystem=strict is read-only bind mounts; MemoryMax= and CPUQuota= are cgroup files; NoNewPrivileges=true is no_new_privs. Container mechanisms, with no container.

cards.q: Map six systemd concepts to Kubernetes.
cards.a: Unit file → Deployment/Pod spec; Restart=on-failure → restartPolicy and CrashLoopBackOff; After=/Requires= → init containers and readiness gates; MemoryMax/CPUQuota → resources.limits (the same cgroup files); TimeoutStopSec → terminationGracePeriodSeconds; .timer → CronJob. The differences are cross-machine scheduling and declarative reconciliation.

cards.q: Why is PM2 inside a container usually wrong?
cards.a: It adds a process, obscures the exit code so the orchestrator cannot see your app crashed, duplicates restart logic the orchestrator already has, and breaks signal propagation. One process per container, restart handled by the orchestrator.

cards.q: Diagnose CrashLoopBackOff from an exit code.
cards.a: 137: SIGKILL, usually OOM — check lastState.terminated.reason. 143: SIGTERM. 139: segmentation fault in a native module. 1: your application threw. 127: command not found — a wrong entrypoint path or a missing shared library. And kubectl logs --previous retrieves the dead container's output.

cards.q: Why does Compose's depends_on so often need a wait script?
cards.a: It waits for the container to start, not to be ready — the ordering-versus-readiness distinction. condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck is the built-in fix.

cards.q: What is procfs, and what does it imply about every diagnostic tool?
cards.a: A filesystem with no storage: reading a file calls a kernel function that generates the content at that instant. So ps, top, free, lsof, node exporters, APM agents and container runtimes are all text parsers. There is no privileged metrics API, and cat is always enough.

cards.q: Which per-process file does top read, and what is in it?
cards.a: /proc/<pid>/stat — a single machine-readable line of 52 fields including utime and stime in clock ticks, minor and major faults, and the start time.

cards.q: How do you attribute CPU to one thread inside a Node process?
cards.a: /proc/<pid>/task/ has one subdirectory per thread with the same files, which is what top -H reads.

cards.q: What do /proc/<pid>/stack and wchan give you?
cards.a: The kernel-side stack and the function the process is sleeping in — so for a D-state hang they tell you exactly which kernel operation it is stuck in.

cards.q: Why is every CPU percentage you have ever seen a derived number?
cards.a: /proc/stat holds cumulative counters since boot, not percentages. A tool samples it twice and divides the deltas — which is why a tool's first sample is meaningless and why average-since-boot is a different and usually useless number.

cards.q: Name four system-wide files and what each answers.
cards.a: /proc/meminfo (what free formats — read MemAvailable); /proc/loadavg (which counts R and D tasks); /proc/interrupts (per-IRQ per-core counts, for interrupt balance); /proc/net/tcp (every socket with state and queue depths, what ss reads).

cards.q: What is /proc/sys and what is its relationship to sysctl?
cards.a: The writable half of procfs — every sysctl is a file there. sysctl -w is a file write; /etc/sysctl.d/ makes it survive a reboot.

cards.q: Where do container CPU, memory and throttling metrics actually come from?
cards.a: cgroup files under /sys/fs/cgroup: memory.current, cpu.stat's nr_throttled. cAdvisor reads them; there is no other source behind your Grafana panel.

cards.q: Why does the JVM need container support and Node need availableParallelism()?
cards.a: /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/meminfo are not namespaced and report the host's values, so any runtime sizing itself from them is wrong inside a container. The correct source is cgroup files; lxcfs exists to present a namespace-correct /proc.

cards.q: Give the six-command sequence that distinguishes the five common production failures.
cards.a: grep -E 'State|Threads|VmRSS|ctxt' /proc/$PID/status; ls /proc/$PID/fd | wc -l against grep 'Max open files' /proc/$PID/limits; cat /proc/$PID/stack if in D state; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat; grep -E '^(anon|file) ' /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.stat. Between them: blocked loop, descriptor leak, storage hang, CPU throttling, page-cache memory pressure.

cards.q: Which two custom metrics are most valuable for a containerised Node service?
cards.a: Event loop delay (from monitorEventLoopDelay) and cgroup nr_throttled, side by side. Node cannot tell you the second, so you read the file yourself.

cards.q: How does a debugger set a breakpoint?
cards.a: It writes 0xCC (int3) over the first byte of the target instruction, saving the original. Execution raises an exception, delivered as SIGTRAP, suspending the process. To continue it restores the byte, single-steps, re-inserts, and resumes. A debugger edits your machine code while it runs — possible only because instructions are data.

cards.q: Why is strace unusable for production performance work?
cards.a: ptrace stops the traced process twice per system call, so a syscall-heavy program can slow by an order of magnitude. Excellent for correctness, wrong for performance.

cards.q: Why does strace on another process need sudo?
cards.a: Attaching means reading all its memory, including keys, so it is gated by CAP_SYS_PTRACE and by ptrace_scope, which by default permits attaching only to descendants. In containers this is --cap-add=SYS_PTRACE.

cards.q: How does perf avoid strace's cost?
cards.a: Sampling. The processor's performance monitoring unit raises an interrupt every N events; perf records the instruction pointer and call stack at each, giving a statistical picture at one to two percent overhead.

cards.q: What can perf stat tell you that a wall-clock measurement cannot?
cards.a: Why it is slow. Hardware counters give instructions retired, cache misses per level, branch mispredictions and TLB misses — so a low instructions-per-cycle figure with high cache misses is a memory-layout problem, not an algorithmic one.

cards.q: How do you read a flame graph correctly?
cards.a: Width is the proportion of samples in which a function was on the stack; the vertical axis is stack depth; the left-to-right ordering is alphabetical and means nothing. A wide plateau at the top is a function burning CPU in itself; a wide tower is a deep call path.

cards.q: How is eBPF reconciled with the rule that user code must never run privileged?
cards.a: A verifier statically proves the bytecode terminates, that every memory access is in bounds, and that it calls only permitted helpers, before JIT-compiling it. A proof obligation substituting for a hardware boundary.

cards.q: What does eBPF change about the economics of observability?
cards.a: Aggregation happens in the kernel — a program can compute a latency histogram of every disk I/O and hand you the finished histogram, instead of copying every event to user space. That is what makes it acceptable in production.

cards.q: Name four eBPF tools and what each answers.
cards.a: execsnoop — every process executed, as it happens. biolatency — a histogram of block-device latency. runqlat — how long tasks wait in the run queue, which is the CPU-contention signal utilisation cannot show and where throttling appears. tcplife — connection lifetimes.

cards.q: Name the three layers of Node profiling and what each sees.
cards.a: JavaScript-level (--prof, DevTools, 0x) — your function names, via V8's sampling profiler. Native-level (perf plus --perf-basic-prof so JIT frames resolve) — V8, libuv, addons and the kernel, which the JavaScript profiler cannot see at all. Kernel-level (eBPF) — what it is waiting for.

cards.q: Give the diagnostic sequence for a slow Node service.
cards.a: High event loop delay and high CPU → the JavaScript profiler. High CPU with no JavaScript function accounting for it → perf; the answer is usually GC, JSON, TLS or an addon. Low CPU with high latency → the process is waiting, and eBPF tools say for what.

cards.q: Why is a buffer leak invisible in a heap snapshot, and how do you find it?
cards.a: Those bytes are outside V8's heap. It shows as rising RSS with a flat heap; find it with perf or by auditing addon usage.

cards.q: Why is continuous production profiling now normal?
cards.a: Because sampling costs one to two percent, running it permanently across a fleet is affordable — and it changes the economics: instead of reproducing a problem, you look at what the process was doing when it happened.

cards.q: What is Meltdown, in one sentence, and why did the fix cost so much?
cards.a: Speculative execution let user-mode code read kernel memory — mapped into every process for efficiency — by inferring values through cache timing. KPTI unmaps kernel memory from the user page table, so every syscall now also switches the page table root and disturbs address translation.

cards.q: Name three other speculative-execution mitigations and what each costs.
cards.a: Retpoline/IBRS/IBPB constrain branch prediction across privilege boundaries, adding cost to indirect calls and context switches; MDS and L1TF mitigations flush buffers on transitions; and on some hardware disabling hyperthreading was the only complete answer, halving the apparent core count.

cards.q: When is mitigations=off defensible?
cards.a: On a single-tenant machine running only trusted code. Indefensible on anything running untrusted code, which includes any machine running a browser or a multi-tenant workload. /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/* lists what is being mitigated.

cards.q: Name the three strategies for crossing the boundary less, with an instance of each.
cards.a: Do not cross (the vDSO answers clock_gettime in user mode at ~20 ns); batch (writev, sendfile, buffered output, epoll itself); replace the interface (io_uring).

cards.q: What is sendfile and why is nginx cheaper than an app serving the same file?
cards.a: It copies from one descriptor to another entirely inside the kernel — no copy into user memory and back, which is the actual meaning of zero-copy. The application path copies the bytes twice for no reason.

cards.q: Describe io_uring's structure and its four properties.
cards.a: Two ring buffers shared between the process and the kernel — a submission queue and a completion queue. Many operations per crossing; optionally zero crossings in SQPOLL mode; completion-based rather than readiness-based, which is what makes it work for regular files; and it covers nearly every operation, with chaining.

cards.q: Why is io_uring blocked by some seccomp profiles and disabled in ChromeOS?
cards.a: Its rapid growth in surface area produced a run of serious security vulnerabilities. Blocking it is done by filtering its syscall numbers — a nice illustration of Node 4.

cards.q: Quantify why syscall count is a design axis in a request handler.
cards.a: 2,000 syscalls at ~100 ns each is 200 µs of pure crossing — ten percent of a 2 ms budget. Hence keeping a log descriptor open, writing a response once rather than forty times, HTTP keep-alive, a Unix socket instead of loopback, and stream.pipeline. strace -c -f gives you the count, and almost nobody takes that measurement.

cards.q: Show that the N+1 query problem is the same optimisation as writev.
cards.a: A syscall crossing is ~100 ns; a local database round trip ~200 µs — two thousand times more. 100 queries is 20 ms of pure round-trip time; one query returning the same rows is 200 µs. DataLoader batching, IN (...), Redis pipelining and HTTP/2 multiplexing are all the same move at a larger scale.

cards.q: State the general principle this node establishes.
cards.a: Every layer has a boundary, and every layer's optimisation is to cross it less often with more in hand. Batch, or move the work to the other side. Those are the only two moves at every scale.

cards.q: What is a monolithic kernel and what are its three properties?
cards.a: All operating system services run in kernel mode in one address space, calling each other as functions. Fast (no boundary crossing between components); fragile (a driver bug can corrupt the page cache, because there is no isolation within one address space); and large — Linux is over 30 million lines, mostly drivers.

cards.q: Do loadable kernel modules provide isolation?
cards.a: No. They still run in kernel mode with full privilege. Modules are a packaging improvement, not an isolation one, and people often assume otherwise.

cards.q: What is a microkernel, and what are its two genuine wins?
cards.a: Only address spaces, threads, scheduling and IPC in kernel mode; filesystems, network stacks and drivers are user-mode servers communicating by messages. Wins: a crashed driver is a restartable process that cannot corrupt what it was not given; and verifiability — seL4, about 10,000 lines, has a machine-checked proof of functional correctness.

cards.q: What is the microkernel's cost, and what reduced it?
cards.a: An operation that was a function call becomes several IPC round trips, each with a context switch and a boundary crossing. Mach (CMU, 1980s) was notably slow; L4 (Liedtke, 1993) cut IPC cost by an order of magnitude and made the argument much closer.

cards.q: Summarise the 1992 Tanenbaum–Torvalds debate accurately.
cards.a: Tanenbaum posted 'LINUX is obsolete' on comp.os.minix, arguing microkernels were the settled research direction and that tying Linux to x86 was short-sighted. Torvalds, then 22, replied that Linux was portable in practice, worked, and was free — that theoretical elegance shipping nothing loses to practical code that runs.

cards.q: Assess that debate thirty years on.
cards.a: Both were right about different things. Tanenbaum was right about reliability and security, borne out by the history of kernel vulnerabilities. Torvalds was right that Linux would win, comprehensively. And microkernel ideas moved rather than lost — FUSE, VFIO and DPDK, gVisor, eBPF and seL4 are all microkernel-flavoured retrofits.

cards.q: Place Linux, Windows NT, XNU, Android and unikernels.
cards.a: Linux: monolithic with modules, stable interface at the syscall boundary. NT: a hybrid whose graphics moved into the kernel in NT 4.0 for speed, at a real cost in stability; stable interface at ntdll.dll. XNU: Mach plus BSD, both in kernel mode, now pushing drivers out with DriverKit. Android: Linux kernel with Bionic, ART, Binder IPC, and one UID per application. Unikernels: no user/kernel split at all, application and OS compiled into one binary.

cards.q: Why is a container escape a consequence of monolithic design?
cards.a: One kernel with 30 million lines of attack surface, shared by every container, called into directly. That is the entire argument for gVisor, Kata and Firecracker, each of which is a different point on this spectrum.

cards.q: Map the microkernel debate onto microservices, with numbers.
cards.a: A monolith is one address space with function calls: fast, simple to deploy, no fault containment. Microservices are separate processes exchanging messages: independently deployable, failures contained, and every internal call becomes ~200 µs instead of ~20 ns — four orders of magnitude, exactly the microkernel's IPC penalty. The likely resolution is the same: mostly monolithic, with boundaries where isolation earns its cost.

cards.q: What happened in 1936, 1945, 1947 and 1948–49?
cards.a: Turing's universal machine paper; the EDVAC draft describing the stored-program design; the transistor at Bell Labs; and the first stored-program executions — the Manchester Baby on 21 June 1948 and EDSAC on 6 May 1949.

cards.q: Name the four systems from 1961–65 and what each contributed.
cards.a: CTSS (MIT, 1961, Corbató): interactive time-sharing and the multi-level feedback queue. Atlas (Manchester, 1962, Kilburn): interrupts with priorities, extracodes, a Supervisor, and demand-paged virtual memory. System/360 (IBM, 1964): one architecture across a line, the 8-bit byte, and JCL. Multics (1965): protection rings, a hierarchical filesystem, dynamic linking, security as a goal.

cards.q: Why is 1973 the decisive year for Unix?
cards.a: It was rewritten in C. An operating system in a high-level language can be moved to a new machine by writing a compiler, and portability — not design — is what actually spread it.

cards.q: How did an antitrust decree shape modern computing?
cards.a: A 1956 consent decree barred AT&T from selling computer products, so Unix was licensed to universities for a nominal fee with source. A generation learned operating systems by reading it.

cards.q: What did 4.2BSD (1983) contribute, and what else happened that year?
cards.a: The socket API and TCP/IP — which is why the internet speaks Unix. The same year Stallman announced GNU, which produced GCC, Emacs and the utilities but never finished its kernel.

cards.q: Name the three things that happened to Linux in 1991–92.
cards.a: Torvalds's 25 August 1991 post and version 0.01 in September; relicensing under the GPL in 1992, which made contribution safe; and the Tanenbaum debate. Also 1992: AT&T's lawsuit against BSDi put the BSDs under a legal cloud for two years — exactly the window in which Linux gathered its community.

cards.q: Name five things from 2003–2009 and what each responded to.
cards.a: Linux 2.6 with the O(1) scheduler and NPTL (2003); nginx (2004), written against C10K; VT-x and AMD-V (2005), making virtualisation practical; EC2 (2006), changing the economics of computing; cgroups merged (2008) from Google; and Node.js at JSConf EU (November 2009).

cards.q: What was Docker's actual contribution in March 2013?
cards.a: Not the kernel features — namespaces since 2002, cgroups since 2008, union filesystems for years. The image format, the registry, and the developer experience: making an assembly of existing kernel features usable in an afternoon. That is a genuine and sufficient contribution.

cards.q: Why is January 2018 a landmark date?
cards.a: Meltdown and Spectre: the first time a processor optimisation forced a coordinated redesign across every operating system, browser and cloud simultaneously.

cards.q: State the three patterns in this history.
cards.a: The ideas were essentially finished by 1970 and everything since is engineering, scale and economics. Licensing and litigation decided outcomes at least as much as design. And simple things that ship beat elegant things that do not — Unix over Multics, Linux over Hurd, Docker over seven prior container systems.

cards.q: Trace a mouse click from the contact to your React handler.
cards.a: Contact closes → USB controller interrupt → kernel input subsystem writes to /dev/input/eventN → the display server wakes from epoll_wait, is scheduled, and routes it → over a Unix socket to the browser UI process → IPC to the owning renderer process (a real process because of Site Isolation) → the renderer's event loop takes it as a task, hit-tests the layout tree, constructs a MouseEvent and dispatches it → React's root listener routes it to onClick.

cards.q: Trace the server side from packet arrival to your route handler.
cards.a: NIC DMAs the packet and raises MSI-X → driver top half schedules NET_RX softirq → softirq walks netfilter (Service IP rewritten to a pod IP), IP and TCP, appending to a socket buffer → the wait-queue callback pushes the descriptor onto epoll's ready list → your process is marked runnable, scheduled subject to its cgroup, and context-switched in → epoll_wait returns in the poll phase → libuv calls back → read() into a Buffer outside the V8 heap → HTTP parser → V8 → your handler.

cards.q: Where exactly does the event loop architecture pay for itself in a request?
cards.a: At the await on the database: the function suspends, a promise is returned, the query is written to a socket, and the loop serves other connections instead of a thread sitting blocked.

cards.q: Trace a query inside Postgres, in mechanism terms.
cards.a: A pooled connection (because Postgres is process-per-connection); a backend wakes; the planner chooses using cost constants encoding disk physics; execution reads from shared_buffers (a shared mapping), falling through to the page cache and then to a real disk read during which the backend is in D state; shared structures are protected by lightweight locks that are futexes; a write appends to the WAL and fsyncs at commit — the largest cost in the transaction.

cards.q: Trace the response from res.json to photons.
cards.a: JSON.stringify runs synchronously, blocking every connection in the process; the write may return short, registering for writability; short-lived objects are scavenged in under a millisecond; packets traverse back through interrupt, softirq, TCP, the browser's network process and IPC to the renderer; the promise resolves as a microtask; React schedules a render in a lane, yielding every ~5 ms; at the next frame boundary rAF, style, layout, compositing and paint run; tiles go to the GPU; the display controller DMAs the framebuffer out sixty times a second.

cards.q: What is the actual value of knowing the forty-five-step trace?
cards.a: 'The API is slow' is not a diagnosis. The list is the complete set of places the time can be, which turns guessing into enumeration.

cards.q: Trace the deployment lifecycle from commit to serving traffic.
cards.a: Editor write to the page cache; content-addressed Git objects; TLS push; a CI runner (a resident monitor) picks up the job in a container; npm ci creates a hundred thousand inodes and compiles addons against that image's libc; a bundler links modules; each Dockerfile instruction becomes an overlayfs layer; layers push to a registry by digest; the scheduler places pods by requests; the kubelet pulls, assembles the overlay, writes cgroup files, clones with namespace flags, wires a veth, pivot_roots, mounts /proc, sets the UID, drops capabilities, installs seccomp and execs; the dynamic linker maps libc and addons; pages fault in; V8 restores from a snapshot; the process listens and then blocks in epoll_wait; the readiness probe passes and kube-proxy programs netfilter; the old pod gets SIGTERM concurrently with endpoint removal.

cards.q: Name the six recurring forces.
cards.a: Sharing, protection, indirection, latency, the boundary, and compatibility.

cards.q: What are the only three answers to a sharing problem?
cards.a: Time-slice it, space-partition it, or queue for it — which are the scheduler, virtual memory, and every queue in your stack.

cards.q: State the protection rule that recurs at every layer.
cards.a: Enforcement must be below the level the protected party can reach. It is why the mode bit is hardware, why WebAssembly bounds-checks in the runtime, why eBPF has a verifier, and why Site Isolation moved to process boundaries.

cards.q: Name eight indirections and the two questions to ask about a new one.
cards.a: Virtual addresses, file descriptors, inodes, PIDs, namespaces, the VFS, sonames and the GOT, and Service IPs. Ask: what does it let the system change without telling anyone, and where is its cache?

cards.q: Name the three techniques for hiding latency and the two problems they all create.
cards.a: Cache, buffer, overlap. Every one creates staleness (what if the cached copy is wrong?) and durability (what if we crash before the buffer drains?) — which is why cache invalidation and fsync are hard in the same way.

cards.q: Give six fossils in modern computing and their causes.
cards.a: The 8-bit byte (System/360); 4 KB pages (the VAX, 1977); the 1024 descriptor default (select's bitmap); port 1024 as the privilege line; the Unix epoch and 2038; and SIGSEGV named for a memory scheme no longer used. Interfaces outlive their reasons because the cost of change is borne by everyone and the benefit by no one.

cards.q: What is the seventh force, not in the list?
cards.a: Licensing, litigation and economics — the AT&T decree, the GPL, the BSD lawsuit, the CDDL keeping ZFS out of the kernel, and EC2's pricing model. None of it is in the mechanisms, and all of it determined which mechanisms you use.

cards.q: What six questions should you ask about a mechanism you have never seen?
cards.a: Which resource is shared and how? What stops one user harming another, and is enforcement below their reach? What is the name and what is the real thing, and where is the translation cached? Which slow thing is hidden, and what goes stale or gets lost? Which boundary is crossed, and what is the batching story? And what is the way it is only because of something in 1977?
